name: The Talking Tree of Newstead House

location.address: Entrance driveway roundabout, Newstead Park, 191A Breakfast Creek Road, Newstead QLD 4006

verified_sources: https://apps.des.qld.gov.au/heritage-register/detail/?id=600265 (Queensland Heritage Register, Newstead House and Park listing, entry 1992-10-21)
access: Free. Stands in the circular garden bed on the entrance driveway roundabout inside Newstead Park, a public Brisbane City Council park with no gate or fee; Newstead House itself (the museum building) is separately ticketed and open Friday to Sunday, but the tree is outside on the public drive, not inside the ticketed grounds.
transport: Breakfast Creek Rd at Evelyn St bus stop (routes 227, 300), about 2 minutes' walk. Bowen Hills rail station is about 9 minutes' walk; Teneriffe CityCat ferry terminal about 16 minutes' walk.
verify_notes: Predates Newstead House itself (established 1846 on the site by Patrick Leslie); already a large fig tree when the house was built, per ABC Gardening Australia's segment on the property (fetched directly, quotes the head gardener: 'it was there before the house was built... over 200 years old'). Sits in the centre of the circular garden roundabout on the entrance driveway ascending from the park's south-west corner toward the house; a speaker in the garden bed plays a recorded history to passers-by, hence the local nickname 'the talking tree' / 'talking history tree' (attested independently in a Flickr caption '83 The talking Tree at Newstead House' and multiple tourist write-ups, e.g. a Tripadvisor photo captioned 'Historic fig tree too'). The Queensland Heritage Register listing for Newstead House and Park (id 600265) describes 'a circular garden roundabout containing a giant fig tree... a magnificent hollowed out Cunningham fig believed to be 200 years old' per a WebSearch-returned extract of that page; I could not independently re-fetch the live apps.des.qld.gov.au page myself (it 301-redirects to a JS-rendered app, qhr.detsi.qld.gov.au, that returned no readable content to WebFetch or curl), so treat that specific quoted extract as corroboration rather than a directly-verified primary read; the ABC Gardening Australia source alone is a solid, directly-fetched, independent second source for species/age/location. One source (a gardening blog snippet found via search, not independently verified) states 'ficus infectoria' as a synonym rather than the primary name; Ficus virens is used consistently across the stronger sources (ABC, the heritage register text, 360Cities photo caption) and is treated as canonical. Age is a source-repeated estimate ('over 200 years', one weaker mention says 'or even 300') rather than a derived one; no girth or planting-date record found. Hollow trunk, so any age-from-girth calculation would be unreliable even if a girth were found; leave as a vague source estimate per the rule against sharpening vague ages. Location: I matched this tree to Brisbane City Council's own 'significant landscape tree' overlay (data/registers/brisbane-significant-landscape-trees.json, objectid 34398, CC BY 4.0, polygon centroid), which sits about 200m from Newstead House's own published coordinates and is by far the closest of the 558 overlay points to this site (next closest cluster of points also sits within 0.5-0.9km, unexplored). This is a plausible but NOT source-confirmed identity match (the overlay carries no name or species field to join on), so location_precision is 'approximate' rather than 'confirmed': the pin is the council's own designated-tree polygon centroid nearest the documented site, not a tree-level coordinate I verified against a named source. A future pass with time to view Brisbane City Council's GIS viewer or a street-level photo could firm this to confirmed. Not the same tree as any of bne_002 to bne_015 (all City Botanic Gardens); this is a genuinely separate site, about 3.8km from the Botanic Gardens cluster by road, not walkable from it, but its own single well-documented destination, not part of any existing cluster.
